documents.text: The cat sat on the mat.
The dog played with the ball.
The cat and dog are friends.

beginner_explanation: TF-IDF helps find important words in a document by checking how often a word appears in that document versus how rare it is across all documents. Common words like 'the' get low scores, unique words get high scores.
advanced_explanation: TF-IDF (Term Frequency-Inverse Document Frequency) weighs terms by their frequency in a document (TF) and inversely by their frequency across documents (IDF). It transforms text into a numerical vector space where similar documents are close together. TF-IDF is computed as TF(t,d) × IDF(t), where IDF(t) = log(N / df(t)).

formula_cards.title: Term Frequency (TF)
formula_cards.explanation: TF measures how frequently a term t appears in document d, normalized by the total number of terms in d.

variables.f_{t,d}: raw frequency of term t in document d

formula_cards.title: Inverse Document Frequency (IDF)
formula_cards.explanation: IDF measures how rare a term is across all N documents. Rare terms get higher IDF scores.

variables.df(t): number of documents containing term t

formula_cards.example: With 3 docs, if 'cat' appears in 2 docs: IDF('cat') = log(3/2) ≈ 0.405

formula_cards.title: TF-IDF Score
formula_cards.explanation: The final TF-IDF score combines term frequency and inverse document frequency.

step_explanations.title: Validate Document Collection
step_explanations.description: Ensure at least one document is provided and all documents have valid text.
step_explanations.why_it_matters: TF-IDF requires multiple documents to compute meaningful IDF scores. Single-document input produces degenerate results.

step_explanations.title: Tokenize and Build Vocabulary
step_explanations.description: Tokenize each document and build a global vocabulary of unique terms.
step_explanations.why_it_matters: The vocabulary defines the feature space dimension. Larger vocabularies capture more information but increase computational cost.

step_explanations.title: Compute Term Frequencies (TF)
step_explanations.description: Calculate how often each term appears in each document, normalized by document length.
step_explanations.why_it_matters: TF captures local importance - terms that appear frequently in a document are likely important to that document's topic.

step_explanations.title: Compute Inverse Document Frequency (IDF)
step_explanations.description: Calculate how rare each term is across all documents. Rare terms get higher scores.
step_explanations.why_it_matters: IDF downweights common words (like 'the') that appear in every document and don't help distinguish topics.

step_explanations.title: Compute TF-IDF Matrix
step_explanations.description: Multiply TF and IDF scores element-wise to get the final TF-IDF matrix.
step_explanations.why_it_matters: The TF-IDF matrix is a numerical representation of documents that can be used for clustering, classification, and similarity search.

hover_annotations.definition: Term Frequency - how often a term appears in a document.
hover_annotations.example: If 'cat' appears 2 times in a 10-word doc, TF = 0.2
hover_annotations.common_mistake: Forgetting to normalize by document length (raw counts bias long documents)

hover_annotations.definition: Inverse Document Frequency - measures term rarity across documents.
hover_annotations.formula_meaning: IDF(t) = log(N / df(t)) where N is total docs and df(t) is docs containing t
hover_annotations.example: If 'cat' is in 2 of 3 docs, IDF = log(3/2) ≈ 0.405
hover_annotations.common_mistake: Using log without smoothing (add 1 to df to avoid division by zero)

hover_annotations.definition: A matrix where rows are documents and columns are terms, with TF-IDF scores as values.
hover_annotations.example: 3 docs × 7 terms = 3×7 matrix with TF-IDF scores
hover_annotations.common_mistake: Thinking higher values always mean more important (context matters)

receiver_mode_explanations.explanation: TF-IDF finds important words by checking: Is this word common in this document? Is it rare across all documents?
receiver_mode_explanations.teaching_notes: Start with 3 simple documents. Show how 'the' gets a low score and unique words get high scores.

receiver_mode_explanations.explanation: TF-IDF = Term Frequency × Inverse Document Frequency. Formula: TF(t,d) × log(N/df(t)).
receiver_mode_explanations.technical_detail: TF normalizes by document length. IDF uses log to dampen the effect of very rare terms. Smoothing: IDF = log((N+1)/(df+1)) + 1.

receiver_mode_explanations.explanation: TF-IDF assumes term independence and doesn't capture semantics. It's a bag-of-words approach. Research shows BM25 (a TF-IDF variant) often outperforms vanilla TF-IDF for retrieval.
receiver_mode_explanations.technical_detail: Limitations: no term ordering, no semantic similarity, sensitive to document length. Variants: BM25, TF-IDF with cosine normalization, sublinear TF (log(1+tf)).

receiver_mode_explanations.explanation: TF-IDF is O(N×L) where N=docs and L=avg doc length. Sparse matrix storage (scipy.sparse) is essential for large vocabularies. Use sklearn.feature_extraction.text.TfidfVectorizer.
receiver_mode_explanations.technical_detail: Complexity: fit O(NL), transform O(NL). Memory: sparse matrix with shape (N, vocab_size). API returns matrix as list of lists or sparse format.

receiver_mode_explanations.explanation: TF-IDF bridges text and math. Show how changing one document affects all IDF scores. Compare with simple word counts.
receiver_mode_explanations.teaching_notes: Quiz: Why does 'the' get a low TF-IDF score? Exercise: Add a 4th document with only 'cat' - how do IDF scores change? Discuss when TF-IDF works well vs. poorly.

research_context: TF-IDF was introduced by Salton et al. (1975) as part of the vector space model for information retrieval. It remains a strong baseline for text classification and retrieval tasks, though neural embeddings have surpassed it for semantic understanding.

teaching_notes.summary: TF-IDF transforms text into numerical vectors by weighing term frequency against document rarity.
quiz_questions: Why does IDF use log? What would happen without it?
Calculate TF-IDF for 'cat' in a 3-document corpus (hint: draw the table first)
When might TF-IDF fail to capture document similarity?
classroom_demo_tips: Add a document with all common words - watch scores drop
Compare TF-IDF vectors using cosine similarity
common_misconceptions: TF-IDF captures word order (false - it's bag-of-words)
Higher TF-IDF always means more important (false - depends on context and task)
